﻿1st Grade Writing Unit Overview
Six-Week Writing Unit: Teacher Overview
Purpose of the Writing Unit
This six-week writing unit is designed to provide first-grade students with explicit, structured, and developmentally appropriate writing instruction that gradually moves them from teacher-supported practice to independent writing. The unit includes four writing lessons per week for a total of 24 detailed lessons.
Each week intentionally builds toward a final end-of-unit writing product. Students will explore the genre, generate ideas, plan, draft, revise, edit, publish, and reflect on their growth as writers. Although each week has a primary focus, the writing process is recursive. Students will regularly reread, revise, edit, and improve their writing throughout the entire unit rather than waiting until the final weeks.
The overall goal is for students to spend meaningful time writing each day while receiving the modeling, guided practice, feedback, and differentiated support needed to become increasingly independent writers.
________________


Instructional Approach: Gradual Release of Responsibility
The Gradual Release of Responsibility Model will guide instruction throughout the unit.
I Do: Teacher Modeling
The teacher explicitly teaches and models the writing skill. During this portion of the lesson, the teacher thinks aloud so students can hear the decisions writers make.
The teacher will:
* Model the writing process step by step.
* Demonstrate how to use the anchor text or mentor text as a model.
* Write in front of students.
* Explain why writers make specific choices.
* Model how to plan, draft, revise, edit, and solve writing problems.
We Do: Guided and Shared Practice
The teacher and students practice the skill together through shared or interactive writing.
Students will:
* Contribute ideas.
* Orally rehearse sentences.
* Help compose shared writing.
* Discuss possible word choices and details.
* Practice using the skill with teacher support.
You Do: Independent Application
Students independently apply the writing skill to their own developing writing pieces.
Students will:
* Generate and organize their own ideas.
* Write independently.
* Apply the lesson’s writing and grammar skills.
* Reread and improve their work.
* Build toward the final writing product.
The gradual release will occur both within individual lessons and across the six-week unit. During the first weeks, students will receive more modeling, shared writing, oral rehearsal, and scaffolding. As the unit progresses, teacher support will gradually decrease as students assume greater responsibility for planning, writing, revising, editing, and completing the final writing task.
________________


Six-Week Learning Progression
Week 1: Explore the Genre and Generate Ideas
The first week introduces students to the writing genre, purpose, and expectations for the unit.
Students will:
* Explore the anchor text and mentor texts.
* Identify important features of the genre.
* Notice how authors organize and develop writing.
* Generate possible writing ideas.
* Discuss and orally rehearse ideas.
* Participate in shared and interactive writing.
The teacher will provide extensive modeling and support during this week. Students will begin thinking about possible ideas for the final writing task but will not be expected to work independently for long periods.
________________


Week 2: Plan and Organize Writing
During Week 2, students learn that strong writers plan before they begin drafting.
Students will:
* Select a focused writing topic.
* Gather, recall, or research information as appropriate to the genre.
* Use developmentally appropriate graphic organizers.
* Organize ideas in a logical order.
* Orally rehearse ideas before writing.
* Begin planning the final writing piece.
The teacher will model several examples of effective planning and provide guided practice before students begin independently planning their own writing.
________________


Week 3: Draft the Writing
During Week 3, students learn how to turn their plans and ideas into connected sentences.
Students will:
* Use their plans to begin drafting.
* Develop a beginning, middle, and ending appropriate to the genre.
* Write complete and meaningful sentences.
* Add relevant details.
* Use the anchor text and mentor texts as models.
* Draft sections of the final writing piece.
Students will continue to receive teacher modeling and guided practice, but they will begin taking greater responsibility for their own writing.
________________


Week 4: Strengthen and Revise Writing
During Week 4, students learn that writers reread and improve their work.
Students will:
* Reread writing for meaning.
* Add important details.
* Remove unnecessary information.
* Rearrange ideas when needed.
* Improve word choice.
* Strengthen sentence development.
* Use feedback from the teacher and peers.
Students will continue developing the final writing piece while learning that revision means making writing clearer, stronger, and more interesting.
________________


Week 5: Edit and Improve Writing
During Week 5, students focus more closely on grammar and conventions while continuing to revise their ideas.
Students will:
* Apply previously taught grammar skills.
* Check for complete sentences.
* Edit capitalization and punctuation.
* Check spelling using developmentally appropriate strategies.
* Use an age-appropriate editing checklist.
* Participate in teacher-student writing conferences.
* Prepare a revised and edited draft of the final writing piece.
Grammar instruction will remain directly connected to students’ writing rather than being taught as an isolated activity.
________________


Week 6: Complete, Publish, and Share
During the final week, students complete and celebrate their writing.
Students will:
* Make final revisions and edits.
* Publish the completed writing product.
* Use the end-of-unit writing rubric for self-assessment.
* Share their writing with an authentic audience.
* Reflect on their growth as writers.
The teacher will use the end-of-unit rubric to assess student progress and identify future writing goals.
________________


Weekly Planning Expectations
Each week of the unit will begin with a clear overview to help teachers understand where students are in the writing process and how the week connects to the final writing product.
Every weekly plan will include:
* Weekly Writing Goal
* Student-Friendly Learning Target
* Writing Standard(s)
* Writing Rope Strand(s)
* Weekly Essential Question
* Writing Skill or Craft Focus
* Grammar and Conventions Focus
* Anchor Text
* Weekly Mentor Text
* Anchor Chart(s)
* Vocabulary
* Required Materials
* Connection to the End-of-Unit Writing Task
* Weekly Formative Assessment
* Differentiation and Scaffolding
* Teacher Conferencing Focus
* Progress-Monitoring Checkpoint
The anchor text and weekly mentor texts must be intentionally selected to support the writing skill being taught. The weekly plan will explain exactly how each text will be used as a model for student writing.
Teachers should help students understand that they are not simply reading the text for comprehension. They are studying the text as writers by asking questions such as:
* What did the author do?
* Why did the author make this choice?
* How does this make the writing stronger?
* How can we try this technique in our own writing?
________________


Daily Lesson Structure
Each of the 24 lessons will follow a consistent instructional structure. This consistency will help students understand the expectations of the writing workshop and allow more instructional time to be spent on writing.
1. Lesson Title
Each lesson will have a clear, engaging title that communicates the writing skill or purpose of the lesson.
________________


2. Student-Friendly Learning Target
Every lesson will include an “I can” statement that clearly explains what students will learn and do.
The learning target will connect directly to:
* The daily writing skill.
* The weekly writing goal.
* The developing writing piece.
* The final end-of-unit writing task.
________________


3. Writing Skill or Craft Focus
Each lesson will focus on one manageable writing skill.
Examples may include:
* Generating ideas.
* Choosing a focused topic.
* Organizing ideas.
* Writing a strong beginning.
* Adding relevant details.
* Using precise words.
* Writing an effective ending.
* Rereading for meaning.
* Revising a sentence.
The focus should be narrow enough for first-grade students to understand, practice, and apply during the same lesson.
________________


4. Grammar and Conventions Connection
Grammar instruction will be brief, purposeful, and directly connected to student writing.
Grammar should not be taught as a separate activity that ends when the worksheet is completed. Students should immediately apply the grammar skill to their current writing.
For example:
* After learning about adjectives, students add adjectives to improve details.
* After reviewing capitalization, students edit their writing for capital letters.
* After learning conjunctions, students combine ideas in their own writing.
* After reviewing punctuation, students reread and edit their sentences.
The goal is for students to understand that grammar and conventions are tools writers use to communicate clearly.
________________


5. Anchor Text or Mentor Text Connection
Every lesson will intentionally connect reading and writing instruction.
The lesson will identify:
* The specific text being used.
* The page, paragraph, sentence, illustration, or section to study.
* What students should notice.
* How the author demonstrates the writing skill.
* How students will apply the author’s technique to their own writing.
Students should be encouraged to view authors as writing mentors whose work can help them make decisions in their own writing.
________________


6. Anchor Chart
Anchor charts will make the writing process and writing strategies visible to students.
Each lesson will identify:
* The title of the anchor chart.
* The key information to include.
* How the teacher will create or use the chart.
Some anchor charts will be created gradually with students during instruction. Others will be introduced as tools and revisited throughout the unit.
Teachers should avoid creating a new chart simply for the sake of having one. Previously developed charts should be revisited whenever they support the current writing work.
________________


7. Explicit Instruction Through Gradual Release
Each lesson will include the following instructional sequence:
I Do: Teacher Modeling
The teacher:
* Models the writing skill.
* Think aloud.
* Writes in front of students.
* Shows the process step by step.
* Makes writing decisions visible.
Students should hear specific language such as:
“I am going to reread my sentence because writers make sure their words say exactly what they mean.”
We Do: Guided or Shared Practice
The teacher and students practice together.
Students may:
* Suggest ideas.
* Orally rehearse sentences.
* Help select details.
* Participate in shared writing.
* Explain which writing choice is strongest.
The teacher uses questions and prompts to guide thinking.
You Do: Independent Writing
Students apply the skill to their own writing.
The independent task will always connect to students’ developing end-of-unit writing pieces whenever appropriate.
________________


Protected Daily Writing Time
Students should spend more time writing than completing worksheets.
Each lesson will include protected writing time. A typical writing period may include:
* 5 minutes: Planning, partner talk, or oral rehearsal.
* 15–20 minutes: Independent writing.
* 5 minutes: Rereading, revising, editing, or reflecting.
The exact amount of time may vary depending on the lesson, but students should have daily opportunities to make meaningful progress on their writing.
The teacher should use this time to:
* Observe students.
* Conduct individual conferences.
* Work with small groups.
* Collect formative assessment information.
* Provide targeted support without taking over the writing.
________________


Teacher-Student Writing Conferences
Conferencing is an essential part of the unit and should occur throughout all six weeks.
Each daily lesson will identify:
* Which students or groups the teacher should meet with.
* The focus of the conference.
* Two or three possible questions or prompts.
* What the teacher should look for in student writing.
* A possible teaching point based on student need.
The following conference structure will be used:
Research
Learn what the student is doing.
“Tell me about what you are working on.”
Notice
Identify and name something the student is already doing well.
“I noticed that you added two details that help your reader understand your topic.”
Teach
Provide one clear, manageable teaching point.
“Today, I want to show you how to reread your sentence and add one word that makes the detail clearer.”
Link
Help the student understand how to use the skill independently.
“Whenever you finish a sentence, reread it and ask yourself whether your reader needs one more detail.”
The goal of a conference is not to correct every error. The goal is to teach one skill that the student can continue using independently.
________________


Revision and Editing Throughout the Unit
Revision and editing should not be limited to Week 5.
Beginning early in the unit, students will regularly reread and improve their writing.
Students may:
* Add details.
* Remove unnecessary information.
* Change words.
* Rearrange ideas.
* Check whether sentences make sense.
* Improve sentence development.
* Edit capitalization.
* Edit punctuation.
* Check spelling.
* Apply the weekly grammar skill.
Teachers should help students understand the difference between the two processes:
Revision asks, “How can I make my ideas stronger or clearer?”
Editing asks, “How can I make my writing correct and easy to read?”
________________


Differentiation and Scaffolding
All students will work toward the same overall writing goal, but the level of support and complexity may differ.
Emerging Writers
Possible supports include:
* Oral rehearsal.
* Drawing before writing.
* Sentence stems.
* Picture supports.
* Word banks.
* Partially completed graphic organizers.
* Teacher or adult scribing when appropriate.
* Small-group reteaching.
On-Level Writers
Students will receive:
* Grade-level graphic organizers.
* Partner rehearsal.
* Access to anchor charts and word banks.
* Teacher conferencing.
* Opportunities to revise and elaborate independently.
Advanced Writers
Challenge opportunities may include:
* Adding more precise or sophisticated details.
* Varying sentence structure.
* Expanding ideas.
* Using stronger transitions.
* Creating more developed beginnings or endings.
* Applying mentor-author techniques independently.
English Learners
Possible supports include:
* Visual vocabulary.
* Picture supports.
* Oral rehearsal.
* Partner talk.
* Sentence frames.
* Repeated modeling.
* Opportunities to say the sentence before writing it.
Students Needing Fine-Motor, Spelling, or Sentence-Development Support
Possible supports include:
* Alternative writing tools.
* Reduced copying demands.
* Alphabet and sound charts.
* Personal word banks.
* Speech-to-text or teacher scribing when appropriate.
* Oral rehearsal.
* Sentence-building cards.
* Small-group instruction.
Differentiation should provide access to the writing process without lowering the purpose or importance of the writing task.
________________


Formative Assessment and Progress Monitoring
Assessment will occur throughout the unit rather than only at the end.
Each lesson will identify exactly what the teacher should collect, observe, or listen for.
Examples include:
* A writing sample.
* An oral response.
* A completed plan.
* One drafted paragraph or section.
* One revised sentence.
* An editing checklist.
* Teacher conference notes.
* An exit ticket.
* A student self-assessment.
At the end of each week, the teacher will use a progress-monitoring checkpoint to determine:
1. What students can do independently.
2. Which skills require additional modeling.
3. Which students need small-group instruction.
4. Which students are ready for greater independence or challenge.
5. Whether students are making adequate progress toward the final writing task.
This information should guide the following week’s instruction, conferencing, and differentiation.
________________


Daily Closing and Reflection
Each lesson will end with a brief opportunity for students to reflect on or share their writing.
Possible closing activities include:
* Partner sharing.
* Author’s chair.
* Reading one improved sentence.
* Naming a revision.
* Showing where the grammar skill was applied.
* Responding to a brief reflection question.
* Setting a goal for the next writing session.
The closing should reinforce the lesson’s learning target and help students recognize their growth as writers.
________________


The Teacher’s Role Across the Six Weeks
The teacher’s role will gradually shift across the unit.
At the Beginning of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Model extensively.
* Think aloud.
* Lead shared writing.
* Provide oral rehearsal.
* Offer sentence stems and visual supports.
* Guide students through each step.
During the Middle of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Continue modeling new skills.
* Provide targeted small-group support.
* Conduct individual conferences.
* Encourage students to use established tools independently.
* Gradually reduce unnecessary support.
At the End of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Encourage student independence.
* Provide feedback rather than taking over the writing.
* Support students in making their own revision and editing decisions.
* Use conferences for targeted teaching points.
* Guide students through self-assessment, publishing, and reflection.
By the end of the six weeks, students should demonstrate greater independence and confidence as they complete a final writing product that reflects the skills developed throughout the unit.
________________


Final Goal
The purpose of this six-week structure is not simply to produce one finished writing piece. The larger goal is to help students develop an understanding of how writers work.
By the end of the unit, students should understand that writers:
* Study other authors.
* Generate and talk through ideas.
* Make a plan.
* Draft one part at a time.
* Reread their work.
* Revise to make ideas stronger.
* Use grammar and conventions to communicate clearly.
* Seek and use feedback.
* Edit carefully.
* Publish and share their work.
* Reflect on their growth.
Each of the 24 lessons should contribute to this larger goal while intentionally moving students toward successful completion of the end-of-unit writing task.

	Unit Title: Evaluate manuscript handwriting. 
Foundational Standards:
* Basic strokes form the foundation of manuscript handwriting.
Unit Vocabulary:
* Headline
* Midline
* Baseline
Materials:
* Lined handwriting paper (newsprint)
* Chart Paper
Unit Procedure (Weekly Days Overview):
Each lesson spans four days, focusing on formation of letters. Each lesson is designed for approximately 10 -15 minutes of instruction.The final day is for review and assessment.
Day 1:Evaluate/Pretest  (15 mins.)
* Model: Write or display the  letters of the alphabet on the board or chart paper. As you point to the letters, invite students to sing the ABC song with you. Tell students that during handwriting they will be learning to write the letters of the alphabet and numbers appropriately. 
* Practice:
   * Explain to students that they will show you how well they can write. Discuss with students the importance of  writing neatly (legibility). 
   * Provide students with a sheet of lined paper for students to write the letters and numbers that they know. 
* Wrap Up/Recap: As students write, take notes of their handwriting skills and areas that you need to support. 
   * Use the Mastery Behaviors checklist to assess student progress. 
   * Keep this sample to compare student handwriting BOY, MOY, and EOY.
Day 2: Handwriting Paper  (10 mins.)
* Model:
   * Explain to students that when we write we have special lines on our writing paper that help us make our letters look neat and tidy.
   * Display for students sheet of lined handwriting paper (preferably chart paper or newsprint, with blue headline, dashed blue midline, and red endline). 
   * The Headline- this line is at the very top. Some of our letters are super tall and touch the headline. Ask students if they can think of a letter that goes all the way to the top (b,d, f, h, k, l, t). Model writing these letters.
   * The Midline- this line is in the middle and it is different- it’s a dashed line. Some of our letters are short and only go up to the midline. They’re short and do not peek over (a, c, e, i, m, n, o, r, s, u, v, w, x, z).  Model writing a few of these letters. 
   * The Red Endline- this line is at the bottom. This line is known as the “endline.” Some of our letters rest on the endline while there will be others that will go under the endline (a, c, e, - under the endline- j, g, y). 
* Guide:
   * Guide students through using handwriting paper to make the basic strokes. Some strokes should start at the headline or midline.
* Practice:
   * Have students practice tracing the basic strokes on the handwriting paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: What did we learn today? What are the names of each line on the paper. 
Day 3:  Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes- Vertical Lines (10 mins.)
* Model:  
   * Explain that pull down lines are called vertical lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a vertical line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters H,D,E,t, b, i, 9, 4. Ask them what each have in common (vertical lines)
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
* Practice:
   * Have students practice writing letters that have vertical lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 4: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Horizontal Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review with students the lines on the paper. 
* Model:  
   * Explain that side to side lines are called horizontal lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a horizontal line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters F, G, B, z,f,e,5,7.  Ask them what each has in common (horizontal lines).
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite.


* Practice: Have students practice writing letters that have horizontal lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 5: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Circle Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review previously taught handwriting strokes.
   * Model:  
      * Model a backward circle line with the starting point at one o’clock. Model forming circle lines in the air as you say the stroke formation. Have students look at letters O, C, Q, e, c,d, q, 9.  Ask them what each have in common (circle lines). Forward circle lines- R, P, D, b, 5, 3
      * Model forming circle lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
   * Practice:
      * Have students practice writing letters that have circle lines appropriately on the paper
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Differentiation:
Support:
* Create remediation packets/materials for students that need support forming specific letters. 
* For Letter Recognition/Formation: Provide pre-written dotted letters for tracing. Use play-doh or sand trays for tactile letter formation. Use multi-sensory activities (e.g., sky writing, tracing letters on a partner's back).
	Assessment: 
	Assessment (Weekly Assessment): (Independent Practice- possibly completed in small group- take notes using the Handwriting Behaviors Checklist)
Students' progress will be measured by:
* Students ability to follow teacher directions on assessment for the weekly letters. Teachers can also include any previous letters learned. This assessment can be completed whole or small group for teacher monitoring.

	Unit Title: Form legible letters and words in print.
Foundational Standards:
* Form uppercase and lowercase letters and words with accuracy.
Unit Vocabulary:
* Headline
* Midline
* Baseline
Materials:
* Lined handwriting paper (newsprint)
* Chart Paper
Unit Procedure (Weekly Days Overview):
Each lesson spans four days, focusing on formation of letters. Each lesson is designed for approximately 10-15  minutes of instruction.The final day is for review and assessment.
Day 1: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Diagonal Lines  (15 mins.)
* Review previously taught handwriting strokes.
* Model:  
   * Model diagonal left and right lines. Explain that diagonal lines slant left and right. Have students look at letters A, N, Q, y, w, z, 2,7. What do you notice about each of these letters?
   * Model forming diagonal lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
* Practice:
   * Have students complete practice writing letters that have diagonal lines in them. 
Day2: Focus on letters L, l, I, i  (15 mins.)
* Model: Write the lowercase l on lined paper or the board as you say the letter formation or display the letter model video. Talk about the shape of the lowercase l. Ask students to name things that look like the letter. .
   * Use skywriting to model l as you repeat the letter formation.  Have students say the letter formation with you as they skywrite.
   * Repeat this process for uppercase L and lowercase/uppercase I. 
* Practice:
   * Students will complete practice pages during independent work time. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 3:  Focus on letter T and ? and !  (10 mins.)
* Model: Write the lowercase t on lined paper or the board as you say the letter formation or display the letter model video. Talk about the shape of the lowercase t. Ask students to name things that look like the letter. .
   * Use skywriting to model t as you repeat the letter formation.  Have students say the letter formation with you as they skywrite.
   * Repeat this process for uppercase T and l? and !. 
* Practice:
   * Students will complete practice pages during independent work time. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 4: Practice L, I, T, ? and !  (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review with students the formation of letters and punctuation marks. 
   * Think aloud as you write words on the board with L, I, and T. Talk through the correct formation of the letters. 
* Practice:
   * Have students practice writing sentences and words. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 5: Focus on Letters  o, O, a, A (10 mins.)
* Model: Write the lowercase o on lined paper or the board as you say the letter formation or display the letter model video. Talk about the shape of the lowercase o.
   * Use skywriting to model o as you repeat the letter formation.  Have students say the letter formation with you as they skywrite.
   * Repeat this process for uppercase O and a, A. 
* Practice:
   * Students will complete practice pages during independent work time. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Differentiation:
Support:
* Create remediation packets/materials for students that need support forming specific letters. 
* For Letter Recognition/Formation: Provide pre-written dotted letters for tracing. Use play-doh or sand trays for tactile letter formation. Use multi-sensory activities (e.g., sky writing, tracing letters on a partner's back).

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Stop, Look, and Save - Writers save details before they write a story.
Model: Model observing the unit visual and writing: "The sun is bright in the daytime sky." Name the common nouns sun and sky.
Think aloud: "I notice the bright sun over Earth. I am going to save the word bright because later, when I write as the sun, I can say, "I shine bright over Earth.""
	Name It Like a Writer - Writers use nouns to name the people, places, and things in a story.
Model: Model sorting sky vocabulary into common nouns: sun, moon, star, cloud, planet, shadow. Write a noun sentence.
Think aloud: "I see sun, moon, cloud, star, and Earth. These are common nouns because they name things. I will write, "A cloud moves across the sky.""
	Two-Source Detective - Writers use both text and pictures to gather information.
Model: Model using a page/spread to record one fact from words and one fact from the visual.
Think aloud: "The words tell me the sun gives Earth light. The picture shows children outside in the daytime. I can use both details later in my story."
	Clue Around the Word - Writers use context clues to understand and use new words.
Model: Model defining a unit word with context clues and a visual. Include affix example: sunny = sun + -y.
Think aloud: "The word warmth is near the sun and the picture shows people outside. I think warmth means heat you can feel. I can write, "Warmth means a gentle heat.""

	Action Steps - Events tell what the narrator does from beginning to end.

Think aloud: "My first event is rise. I can add -s because I am writing what I do: "I rise over Earth." Another event is warm: "I warm the garden.""
	Match the Mark - End punctuation helps readers know how the sentence should sound.
Model: Model adding punctuation to a short sun narrative draft.
Think aloud: ""I shine over Earth" tells something, so it needs a period. "Look at my golden rays" is a command, so it also needs an end mark. "What a bright day!" needs an exclamation point."

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Close the Day - A narrative ending shows the last event or the narrator's final feeling.
Model: Model writing an ending with a last event and feeling: "Finally, I sink behind the hills. I feel proud because Earth is warm and bright."
Think aloud: "My sun has helped Earth all day. At the end, I can set behind the trees and let the moon rise. That shows the day is ending."
	Add a Picture Word - Adjectives make nouns more specific and vivid.
Model: Model finding nouns in the draft and adding adjectives: golden rays, quiet morning, tall trees.
Think aloud: "I wrote "rays." What kind of rays? Golden rays. Warm rays. I will choose golden because it helps my reader see the color."
	Move the Sun - Verbs tell action; prepositions tell where the action happens.
Model: Model revising weak verbs and adding prepositional phrases: over the ocean, behind the hills, across the sky.
Think aloud: "Instead of "I go," I can write "I travel across the sky." Across tells where and travel is stronger than go."
	Choose the Just-Right Word - Writers choose words that match exactly what they mean.
Model: Model using context clues to define a word and using affixes such as sunny, shining, warmed.
Think aloud: "Warm and blazing both describe the sun, but they do not feel the same. If my sun is gentle in the morning, warm is better. If it is very hot, blazing is better."

﻿1st Grade Writing Unit Overview
Six-Week Writing Unit: Teacher Overview
Purpose of the Writing Unit
This six-week writing unit is designed to provide first-grade students with explicit, structured, and developmentally appropriate writing instruction that gradually moves them from teacher-supported practice to independent writing. The unit includes four writing lessons per week for a total of 24 detailed lessons.
Each week intentionally builds toward a final end-of-unit writing product. Students will explore the genre, generate ideas, plan, draft, revise, edit, publish, and reflect on their growth as writers. Although each week has a primary focus, the writing process is recursive. Students will regularly reread, revise, edit, and improve their writing throughout the entire unit rather than waiting until the final weeks.
The overall goal is for students to spend meaningful time writing each day while receiving the modeling, guided practice, feedback, and differentiated support needed to become increasingly independent writers.
________________


Instructional Approach: Gradual Release of Responsibility
The Gradual Release of Responsibility Model will guide instruction throughout the unit.
I Do: Teacher Modeling
The teacher explicitly teaches and models the writing skill. During this portion of the lesson, the teacher thinks aloud so students can hear the decisions writers make.
The teacher will:
* Model the writing process step by step.
* Demonstrate how to use the anchor text or mentor text as a model.
* Write in front of students.
* Explain why writers make specific choices.
* Model how to plan, draft, revise, edit, and solve writing problems.
We Do: Guided and Shared Practice
The teacher and students practice the skill together through shared or interactive writing.
Students will:
* Contribute ideas.
* Orally rehearse sentences.
* Help compose shared writing.
* Discuss possible word choices and details.
* Practice using the skill with teacher support.
You Do: Independent Application
Students independently apply the writing skill to their own developing writing pieces.
Students will:
* Generate and organize their own ideas.
* Write independently.
* Apply the lesson’s writing and grammar skills.
* Reread and improve their work.
* Build toward the final writing product.
The gradual release will occur both within individual lessons and across the six-week unit. During the first weeks, students will receive more modeling, shared writing, oral rehearsal, and scaffolding. As the unit progresses, teacher support will gradually decrease as students assume greater responsibility for planning, writing, revising, editing, and completing the final writing task.
________________


Six-Week Learning Progression
Week 1: Explore the Genre and Generate Ideas
The first week introduces students to the writing genre, purpose, and expectations for the unit.
Students will:
* Explore the anchor text and mentor texts.
* Identify important features of the genre.
* Notice how authors organize and develop writing.
* Generate possible writing ideas.
* Discuss and orally rehearse ideas.
* Participate in shared and interactive writing.
The teacher will provide extensive modeling and support during this week. Students will begin thinking about possible ideas for the final writing task but will not be expected to work independently for long periods.
________________


Week 2: Plan and Organize Writing
During Week 2, students learn that strong writers plan before they begin drafting.
Students will:
* Select a focused writing topic.
* Gather, recall, or research information as appropriate to the genre.
* Use developmentally appropriate graphic organizers.
* Organize ideas in a logical order.
* Orally rehearse ideas before writing.
* Begin planning the final writing piece.
The teacher will model several examples of effective planning and provide guided practice before students begin independently planning their own writing.
________________


Week 3: Draft the Writing
During Week 3, students learn how to turn their plans and ideas into connected sentences.
Students will:
* Use their plans to begin drafting.
* Develop a beginning, middle, and ending appropriate to the genre.
* Write complete and meaningful sentences.
* Add relevant details.
* Use the anchor text and mentor texts as models.
* Draft sections of the final writing piece.
Students will continue to receive teacher modeling and guided practice, but they will begin taking greater responsibility for their own writing.
________________


Week 4: Strengthen and Revise Writing
During Week 4, students learn that writers reread and improve their work.
Students will:
* Reread writing for meaning.
* Add important details.
* Remove unnecessary information.
* Rearrange ideas when needed.
* Improve word choice.
* Strengthen sentence development.
* Use feedback from the teacher and peers.
Students will continue developing the final writing piece while learning that revision means making writing clearer, stronger, and more interesting.
________________


Week 5: Edit and Improve Writing
During Week 5, students focus more closely on grammar and conventions while continuing to revise their ideas.
Students will:
* Apply previously taught grammar skills.
* Check for complete sentences.
* Edit capitalization and punctuation.
* Check spelling using developmentally appropriate strategies.
* Use an age-appropriate editing checklist.
* Participate in teacher-student writing conferences.
* Prepare a revised and edited draft of the final writing piece.
Grammar instruction will remain directly connected to students’ writing rather than being taught as an isolated activity.
________________


Week 6: Complete, Publish, and Share
During the final week, students complete and celebrate their writing.
Students will:
* Make final revisions and edits.
* Publish the completed writing product.
* Use the end-of-unit writing rubric for self-assessment.
* Share their writing with an authentic audience.
* Reflect on their growth as writers.
The teacher will use the end-of-unit rubric to assess student progress and identify future writing goals.
________________


Weekly Planning Expectations
Each week of the unit will begin with a clear overview to help teachers understand where students are in the writing process and how the week connects to the final writing product.
Every weekly plan will include:
* Weekly Writing Goal
* Student-Friendly Learning Target
* Writing Standard(s)
* Writing Rope Strand(s)
* Weekly Essential Question
* Writing Skill or Craft Focus
* Grammar and Conventions Focus
* Anchor Text
* Weekly Mentor Text
* Anchor Chart(s)
* Vocabulary
* Required Materials
* Connection to the End-of-Unit Writing Task
* Weekly Formative Assessment
* Differentiation and Scaffolding
* Teacher Conferencing Focus
* Progress-Monitoring Checkpoint
The anchor text and weekly mentor texts must be intentionally selected to support the writing skill being taught. The weekly plan will explain exactly how each text will be used as a model for student writing.
Teachers should help students understand that they are not simply reading the text for comprehension. They are studying the text as writers by asking questions such as:
* What did the author do?
* Why did the author make this choice?
* How does this make the writing stronger?
* How can we try this technique in our own writing?
________________


Daily Lesson Structure
Each of the 24 lessons will follow a consistent instructional structure. This consistency will help students understand the expectations of the writing workshop and allow more instructional time to be spent on writing.
1. Lesson Title
Each lesson will have a clear, engaging title that communicates the writing skill or purpose of the lesson.
________________


2. Student-Friendly Learning Target
Every lesson will include an “I can” statement that clearly explains what students will learn and do.
The learning target will connect directly to:
* The daily writing skill.
* The weekly writing goal.
* The developing writing piece.
* The final end-of-unit writing task.
________________


3. Writing Skill or Craft Focus
Each lesson will focus on one manageable writing skill.
Examples may include:
* Generating ideas.
* Choosing a focused topic.
* Organizing ideas.
* Writing a strong beginning.
* Adding relevant details.
* Using precise words.
* Writing an effective ending.
* Rereading for meaning.
* Revising a sentence.
The focus should be narrow enough for first-grade students to understand, practice, and apply during the same lesson.
________________


4. Grammar and Conventions Connection
Grammar instruction will be brief, purposeful, and directly connected to student writing.
Grammar should not be taught as a separate activity that ends when the worksheet is completed. Students should immediately apply the grammar skill to their current writing.
For example:
* After learning about adjectives, students add adjectives to improve details.
* After reviewing capitalization, students edit their writing for capital letters.
* After learning conjunctions, students combine ideas in their own writing.
* After reviewing punctuation, students reread and edit their sentences.
The goal is for students to understand that grammar and conventions are tools writers use to communicate clearly.
________________


5. Anchor Text or Mentor Text Connection
Every lesson will intentionally connect reading and writing instruction.
The lesson will identify:
* The specific text being used.
* The page, paragraph, sentence, illustration, or section to study.
* What students should notice.
* How the author demonstrates the writing skill.
* How students will apply the author’s technique to their own writing.
Students should be encouraged to view authors as writing mentors whose work can help them make decisions in their own writing.
________________


6. Anchor Chart
Anchor charts will make the writing process and writing strategies visible to students.
Each lesson will identify:
* The title of the anchor chart.
* The key information to include.
* How the teacher will create or use the chart.
Some anchor charts will be created gradually with students during instruction. Others will be introduced as tools and revisited throughout the unit.
Teachers should avoid creating a new chart simply for the sake of having one. Previously developed charts should be revisited whenever they support the current writing work.
________________


7. Explicit Instruction Through Gradual Release
Each lesson will include the following instructional sequence:
I Do: Teacher Modeling
The teacher:
* Models the writing skill.
* Think aloud.
* Writes in front of students.
* Shows the process step by step.
* Makes writing decisions visible.
Students should hear specific language such as:
“I am going to reread my sentence because writers make sure their words say exactly what they mean.”
We Do: Guided or Shared Practice
The teacher and students practice together.
Students may:
* Suggest ideas.
* Orally rehearse sentences.
* Help select details.
* Participate in shared writing.
* Explain which writing choice is strongest.
The teacher uses questions and prompts to guide thinking.
You Do: Independent Writing
Students apply the skill to their own writing.
The independent task will always connect to students’ developing end-of-unit writing pieces whenever appropriate.
________________


Protected Daily Writing Time
Students should spend more time writing than completing worksheets.
Each lesson will include protected writing time. A typical writing period may include:
* 5 minutes: Planning, partner talk, or oral rehearsal.
* 15–20 minutes: Independent writing.
* 5 minutes: Rereading, revising, editing, or reflecting.
The exact amount of time may vary depending on the lesson, but students should have daily opportunities to make meaningful progress on their writing.
The teacher should use this time to:
* Observe students.
* Conduct individual conferences.
* Work with small groups.
* Collect formative assessment information.
* Provide targeted support without taking over the writing.
________________


Teacher-Student Writing Conferences
Conferencing is an essential part of the unit and should occur throughout all six weeks.
Each daily lesson will identify:
* Which students or groups the teacher should meet with.
* The focus of the conference.
* Two or three possible questions or prompts.
* What the teacher should look for in student writing.
* A possible teaching point based on student need.
The following conference structure will be used:
Research
Learn what the student is doing.
“Tell me about what you are working on.”
Notice
Identify and name something the student is already doing well.
“I noticed that you added two details that help your reader understand your topic.”
Teach
Provide one clear, manageable teaching point.
“Today, I want to show you how to reread your sentence and add one word that makes the detail clearer.”
Link
Help the student understand how to use the skill independently.
“Whenever you finish a sentence, reread it and ask yourself whether your reader needs one more detail.”
The goal of a conference is not to correct every error. The goal is to teach one skill that the student can continue using independently.
________________


Revision and Editing Throughout the Unit
Revision and editing should not be limited to Week 5.
Beginning early in the unit, students will regularly reread and improve their writing.
Students may:
* Add details.
* Remove unnecessary information.
* Change words.
* Rearrange ideas.
* Check whether sentences make sense.
* Improve sentence development.
* Edit capitalization.
* Edit punctuation.
* Check spelling.
* Apply the weekly grammar skill.
Teachers should help students understand the difference between the two processes:
Revision asks, “How can I make my ideas stronger or clearer?”
Editing asks, “How can I make my writing correct and easy to read?”
________________


Differentiation and Scaffolding
All students will work toward the same overall writing goal, but the level of support and complexity may differ.
Emerging Writers
Possible supports include:
* Oral rehearsal.
* Drawing before writing.
* Sentence stems.
* Picture supports.
* Word banks.
* Partially completed graphic organizers.
* Teacher or adult scribing when appropriate.
* Small-group reteaching.
On-Level Writers
Students will receive:
* Grade-level graphic organizers.
* Partner rehearsal.
* Access to anchor charts and word banks.
* Teacher conferencing.
* Opportunities to revise and elaborate independently.
Advanced Writers
Challenge opportunities may include:
* Adding more precise or sophisticated details.
* Varying sentence structure.
* Expanding ideas.
* Using stronger transitions.
* Creating more developed beginnings or endings.
* Applying mentor-author techniques independently.
English Learners
Possible supports include:
* Visual vocabulary.
* Picture supports.
* Oral rehearsal.
* Partner talk.
* Sentence frames.
* Repeated modeling.
* Opportunities to say the sentence before writing it.
Students Needing Fine-Motor, Spelling, or Sentence-Development Support
Possible supports include:
* Alternative writing tools.
* Reduced copying demands.
* Alphabet and sound charts.
* Personal word banks.
* Speech-to-text or teacher scribing when appropriate.
* Oral rehearsal.
* Sentence-building cards.
* Small-group instruction.
Differentiation should provide access to the writing process without lowering the purpose or importance of the writing task.
________________


Formative Assessment and Progress Monitoring
Assessment will occur throughout the unit rather than only at the end.
Each lesson will identify exactly what the teacher should collect, observe, or listen for.
Examples include:
* A writing sample.
* An oral response.
* A completed plan.
* One drafted paragraph or section.
* One revised sentence.
* An editing checklist.
* Teacher conference notes.
* An exit ticket.
* A student self-assessment.
At the end of each week, the teacher will use a progress-monitoring checkpoint to determine:
1. What students can do independently.
2. Which skills require additional modeling.
3. Which students need small-group instruction.
4. Which students are ready for greater independence or challenge.
5. Whether students are making adequate progress toward the final writing task.
This information should guide the following week’s instruction, conferencing, and differentiation.
________________


Daily Closing and Reflection
Each lesson will end with a brief opportunity for students to reflect on or share their writing.
Possible closing activities include:
* Partner sharing.
* Author’s chair.
* Reading one improved sentence.
* Naming a revision.
* Showing where the grammar skill was applied.
* Responding to a brief reflection question.
* Setting a goal for the next writing session.
The closing should reinforce the lesson’s learning target and help students recognize their growth as writers.
________________


The Teacher’s Role Across the Six Weeks
The teacher’s role will gradually shift across the unit.
At the Beginning of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Model extensively.
* Think aloud.
* Lead shared writing.
* Provide oral rehearsal.
* Offer sentence stems and visual supports.
* Guide students through each step.
During the Middle of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Continue modeling new skills.
* Provide targeted small-group support.
* Conduct individual conferences.
* Encourage students to use established tools independently.
* Gradually reduce unnecessary support.
At the End of the Unit
The teacher will:
* Encourage student independence.
* Provide feedback rather than taking over the writing.
* Support students in making their own revision and editing decisions.
* Use conferences for targeted teaching points.
* Guide students through self-assessment, publishing, and reflection.
By the end of the six weeks, students should demonstrate greater independence and confidence as they complete a final writing product that reflects the skills developed throughout the unit.
________________


Final Goal
The purpose of this six-week structure is not simply to produce one finished writing piece. The larger goal is to help students develop an understanding of how writers work.
By the end of the unit, students should understand that writers:
* Study other authors.
* Generate and talk through ideas.
* Make a plan.
* Draft one part at a time.
* Reread their work.
* Revise to make ideas stronger.
* Use grammar and conventions to communicate clearly.
* Seek and use feedback.
* Edit carefully.
* Publish and share their work.
* Reflect on their growth.
Each of the 24 lessons should contribute to this larger goal while intentionally moving students toward successful completion of the end-of-unit writing task.

	Unit Title: Evaluate manuscript handwriting. 
Foundational Standards:
* Basic strokes form the foundation of manuscript handwriting.
Unit Vocabulary:
* Headline
* Midline
* Baseline
Materials:
* Lined handwriting paper (newsprint)
* Chart Paper
Unit Procedure (Weekly Days Overview):
Each lesson spans four days, focusing on formation of letters. Each lesson is designed for approximately 10 -15 minutes of instruction.The final day is for review and assessment.
Day 1:Evaluate/Pretest  (15 mins.)
* Model: Write or display the  letters of the alphabet on the board or chart paper. As you point to the letters, invite students to sing the ABC song with you. Tell students that during handwriting they will be learning to write the letters of the alphabet and numbers appropriately. 
* Practice:
   * Explain to students that they will show you how well they can write. Discuss with students the importance of  writing neatly (legibility). 
   * Provide students with a sheet of lined paper for students to write the letters and numbers that they know. 
* Wrap Up/Recap: As students write, take notes of their handwriting skills and areas that you need to support. 
   * Use the Mastery Behaviors checklist to assess student progress. 
   * Keep this sample to compare student handwriting BOY, MOY, and EOY.
Day 2: Handwriting Paper  (10 mins.)
* Model:
   * Explain to students that when we write we have special lines on our writing paper that help us make our letters look neat and tidy.
   * Display for students sheet of lined handwriting paper (preferably chart paper or newsprint, with blue headline, dashed blue midline, and red endline). 
   * The Headline- this line is at the very top. Some of our letters are super tall and touch the headline. Ask students if they can think of a letter that goes all the way to the top (b,d, f, h, k, l, t). Model writing these letters.
   * The Midline- this line is in the middle and it is different- it’s a dashed line. Some of our letters are short and only go up to the midline. They’re short and do not peek over (a, c, e, i, m, n, o, r, s, u, v, w, x, z).  Model writing a few of these letters. 
   * The Red Endline- this line is at the bottom. This line is known as the “endline.” Some of our letters rest on the endline while there will be others that will go under the endline (a, c, e, - under the endline- j, g, y). 
* Guide:
   * Guide students through using handwriting paper to make the basic strokes. Some strokes should start at the headline or midline.
* Practice:
   * Have students practice tracing the basic strokes on the handwriting paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: What did we learn today? What are the names of each line on the paper. 
Day 3:  Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes- Vertical Lines (10 mins.)
* Model:  
   * Explain that pull down lines are called vertical lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a vertical line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters H,D,E,t, b, i, 9, 4. Ask them what each have in common (vertical lines)
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
* Practice:
   * Have students practice writing letters that have vertical lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 4: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Horizontal Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review with students the lines on the paper. 
* Model:  
   * Explain that side to side lines are called horizontal lines. Ask students to stand up straight. Point out that a horizontal line might be drawn from the top of their head to the bottom of their feet. 
   * Have students look at letters F, G, B, z,f,e,5,7.  Ask them what each has in common (horizontal lines).
   * Model forming vertical lines in the air and have the students skywrite.


* Practice: Have students practice writing letters that have horizontal lines appropriately on the paper. 
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:"What did we learn today? Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Day 5: Review of  Writing Positions and Basic Strokes-Circle Lines (10 mins.)
* Review: 
   * Review previously taught handwriting strokes.
   * Model:  
      * Model a backward circle line with the starting point at one o’clock. Model forming circle lines in the air as you say the stroke formation. Have students look at letters O, C, Q, e, c,d, q, 9.  Ask them what each have in common (circle lines). Forward circle lines- R, P, D, b, 5, 3
      * Model forming circle lines in the air and have the students skywrite. 
   * Practice:
      * Have students practice writing letters that have circle lines appropriately on the paper
* Wrap-up/Recap: 
   * Use these questions for students to evaluate their writing:Is the stroke of your letter touching the right line on the paper (headline, midline, endline)?
Differentiation:
Support:
* Create remediation packets/materials for students that need support forming specific letters. 
* For Letter Recognition/Formation: Provide pre-written dotted letters for tracing. Use play-doh or sand trays for tactile letter formation. Use multi-sensory activities (e.g., sky writing, tracing letters on a partner's back).
	Assessment: 
	Assessment (Weekly Assessment): (Independent Practice- possibly completed in small group- take notes using the Handwriting Behaviors Checklist)
Students' progress will be measured by:
* Students ability to follow teacher directions on assessment for the weekly letters. Teachers can also include any previous letters learned. This assessment can be completed whole or small group for teacher monitoring.

UNIT 1 • Working Together • ANCHOR CHART 1
	Explanatory Writers Teach the Reader
We explain a topic clearly so the reader learns something.
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
	How can people work together to solve problems and help one another?
	FINAL WRITING TASK
	Explain how a character works with others. Use details from the text to teach the reader.
	 
A strong explanation has...
✓ A clear topic
✓ Important details
✓ Ideas in a logical order
✓ A closing that wraps it up
	Writers ask...
✓ What am I teaching?
✓ Which details matter most?
✓ How can I explain my thinking?
✓ Does my ending sound finished?
	 
TRY IT!  SENTENCE FRAMES
My topic is _____.
One important detail is _____.
Another detail is _____.
Now you know _____.
	Explanatory Writing • Read it. Say it. Write it. Reread it.


 
UNIT 1 • Working Together • ANCHOR CHART 2
	How Do Characters Work Together?
Look closely at what the characters say and do.
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
	How can people work together to solve problems and help one another?
	FINAL WRITING TASK
	Explain how a character works with others. Use details from the text to teach the reader.
	 
Notice the teamwork
✓ WHO is working together?
✓ WHAT do they do?
✓ HOW do they help each other?
✓ WHAT happens because they work together?
	Turn actions into explanations
✓ Name the character or group
✓ Tell the action
✓ Explain how the action helps
✓ Connect the detail to teamwork
	 
TRY IT!  SENTENCE FRAMES
_____ works with _____ by _____.
They help each other when _____.
This shows teamwork because _____.
	Explanatory Writing • Read it. Say it. Write it. Reread it.


 
UNIT 1 • Working Together • ANCHOR CHART 3
	Use Text Details to Explain
Good explanations are built from evidence in words and pictures.
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
	How can people work together to solve problems and help one another?
	FINAL WRITING TASK
	Explain how a character works with others. Use details from the text to teach the reader.
	 
1. FIND
✓ Read or look closely
✓ Choose a detail that matches the topic
✓ Point to the words or picture
	2. EXPLAIN
✓ Say the detail in your own words
✓ Tell what the detail shows
✓ Connect it back to the topic
	 
TRY IT!  SENTENCE FRAMES
In the text, _____.
The picture shows _____.
This detail shows that _____.
	Explanatory Writing • Read it. Say it. Write it. Reread it.


 
UNIT 1 • Working Together • ANCHOR CHART 4

	Students Needing Extended Scaffolds
	Provide a picture choice board and oral rehearsal. Accept dictation or a labeled drawing plus one sentence.

	Use a 2-box organizer: character + want. Rehearse aloud before writing.

	Complete one box at a time with teacher prompts.
	Students Who Are Independent
	Add a second possible character or explain why the map matters to the character.

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Notice the Feeling: “The narrator says I and describes too many noises and sights. I infer she feels overwhelmed because the sensory details pile up.” Teacher model: Finish Too Much! Model identifying first-person narrator and underlining sensory clues that reveal the feeling overwhelmed.
	Clue -> Inference: “The character covers her ears and moves away from the crowd. I infer she feels stressed because the loud sounds are too much.” Teacher model: Model a three-part organizer: Clue / My Thinking / Because Sentence. Use a sensory detail from Too Much!
	Read the Setting: “Isamu chooses the quiet ocean. He hears waves and feels stones under his feet. The calm setting shows he likes peaceful places.” Teacher model: Read A Boy Named Isamu (read 1 of 3). Model a setting web with sensory details and one interpretation sentence.
	Evidence Explains My Thinking: “I think Isamu enjoyed being alone. He looked for quiet places in nature. That detail supports my opinion because he chose peaceful places for himself.” Teacher model: Read A Boy Named Isamu (read 2 of 3). Model an opinion about whether Isamu enjoyed being alone, using one story detail and a closing.

	Skill / Strategy Named
	Writing: Analyze Character Feelings Across Events | Language: I can record the story detail that supports each feeling.

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Track the Feeling: “At the beginning Rocio misses home. I record homesick and the clue that she has moved far away. Later, the package changes her feeling.” Teacher model: Read With Lots of Love (read 1 of 3). Model a B-M-E feeling tracker with one accurate clue in each section.
	Infer the Wish: “Rocio could wish to visit home, see Abuela, or feel close to home. I choose to feel close to Abuela because the package of familiar things brings comfort and love.” Teacher model: Read With Lots of Love (read 2 of 3). Model brainstorming two wishes, checking them against the text, and selecting the strongest.
	Choose the Best Proof: “My opinion is that Rocio wished to feel close to her family. The best proof is that she misses home and that Abuela sends familiar things that comfort her.” Teacher model: Read With Lots of Love (read 3 of 3). Model crossing out a weak detail and keeping two details that directly support the selected wish.
	Build the Opinion Frame: “I plan my response in order: how Rocio felt, what I think she wished for, why I think it, and the story details that support me. I do not draft until every box has an idea.” Teacher model: Use the Session 25 A Boy Named Isamu exemplar to label text/title, opinion, reason, evidence, and closing. Then model a Rocio plan without writing the full draft.

	Craft Move / Author Technique Highlighted
	Character feelings often change because of events and relationships.
	More than one inference may be possible, but the writer must support the choice with evidence.
	Strong writers select evidence for relevance, not just because it is memorable.
	Opinion responses are organized so the reader can easily follow the writer’s thinking.

Think aloud: "I see sun, moon, cloud, star, and Earth. These are common nouns because they name things. I will write, "A cloud moves across the sky.""
	Two-Source Detective - Writers use both text and pictures to gather information.
Model: Model using a page/spread to record one fact from words and one fact from the visual.
Think aloud: "The words tell me the sun gives Earth light. The picture shows children outside in the daytime. I can use both details later in my story."
	Clue Around the Word - Writers use context clues to understand and use new words.
Model: Model defining a unit word with context clues and a visual. Include affix example: sunny = sun + -y.
Think aloud: "The word warmth is near the sun and the picture shows people outside. I think warmth means heat you can feel. I can write, "Warmth means a gentle heat.""

	Map the Day - Narrative writers plan events before drafting so the story has order.

	Land the Story - Writers plan a closing event so the story feels finished.
Model: Model adding an ending to the planner and writing a declarative and exclamatory sentence.

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Hook with Who and Where - A strong beginning tells readers who is speaking and where the story starts.
Model: Model drafting 2-3 opening sentences from the story planner.
Think aloud: "I need my reader to know I am the sun. I will write, "I am the sun. Each morning, I peek over the blue hills.""
	Place the Reader - Setting details help readers picture where the story happens.
Model: Model revising a plain setting sentence to include an adjective and a preposition.
Think aloud: "Instead of "I am in the sky," I can write, "I shine above the quiet playground." Above is my preposition and quiet is my adjective."
	Action Steps - Events tell what the narrator does from beginning to end.
Model: Model drafting events using regular verbs: rise/rises, warm/warms, shine/shines, help/helps.
Think aloud: "My first event is rise. I can add -s because I am writing what I do: "I rise over Earth." Another event is warm: "I warm the garden.""
	Match the Mark - End punctuation helps readers know how the sentence should sound.
Model: Model adding punctuation to a short sun narrative draft.
Think aloud: ""I shine over Earth" tells something, so it needs a period. "Look at my golden rays" is a command, so it also needs an end mark. "What a bright day!" needs an exclamation point."

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Close the Day - A narrative ending shows the last event or the narrator's final feeling.
Model: Model writing an ending with a last event and feeling: "Finally, I sink behind the hills. I feel proud because Earth is warm and bright."
Think aloud: "My sun has helped Earth all day. At the end, I can set behind the trees and let the moon rise. That shows the day is ending."
	Add a Picture Word - Adjectives make nouns more specific and vivid.
Model: Model finding nouns in the draft and adding adjectives: golden rays, quiet morning, tall trees.
Think aloud: "I wrote "rays." What kind of rays? Golden rays. Warm rays. I will choose golden because it helps my reader see the color."
	Move the Sun - Verbs tell action; prepositions tell where the action happens.
Model: Model revising weak verbs and adding prepositional phrases: over the ocean, behind the hills, across the sky.
Think aloud: "Instead of "I go," I can write "I travel across the sky." Across tells where and travel is stronger than go."
	Choose the Just-Right Word - Writers choose words that match exactly what they mean.
Model: Model using context clues to define a word and using affixes such as sunny, shining, warmed.
Think aloud: "Warm and blazing both describe the sun, but they do not feel the same. If my sun is gentle in the morning, warm is better. If it is very hot, blazing is better."

	Touch Each Sentence - Editors touch each sentence so they do not skip capitals or end marks.
Model: Model editing a paragraph sentence by sentence for capitals and periods/question marks/exclamation points.
Think aloud: "This sentence starts with "i," but the pronoun I is always capital. I also need a period at the end because it tells something."

Model: Model giving kind, specific feedback and making one final correction.

	Think-Aloud / Demonstration
	Best Work Copy - A final copy helps readers enjoy and understand the story.
Model: Model copying one edited sentence neatly and checking it against the draft.
Think aloud: "I will keep my edited draft beside me. After I copy a sentence, I will reread it to make sure I did not leave out a word."
	Picture Matches Words - Pictures help readers understand the story when they match the writing.
Model: Model turning a sentence into a labeled illustration.
Think aloud: "My story says I warm the ocean. I will draw the sun over the ocean and label sun, rays, ocean, and Earth."
	Read It Proud - Authors use their voice to help the audience hear the story.
Model: Model reading a short passage with expression and responding with warm feedback.
Think aloud: "When I see an exclamation point, I will read with excitement. When I see a period, I will stop and breathe."
	Look Back and Name Growth - Writers grow when they notice what they learned and what they will try next.
Model: Model completing a self-assessment using the rubric.
Think aloud: "My glow is I stayed in I voice. My goal is to use even stronger verbs next time."
